hints: Look for carbon atoms joined to four different groups, remember that $C=O$, $CH_2$ and $CH_3$ carbons can never be chiral, focus on the $CH$ carbons in the chain and the fused ring.
walkthrough:
Apply the four different groups test**
Picture yourself sitting with Fig. 6.1 and putting your finger on each carbon in turn. A chiral carbon must have four single bonds to four completely different groups. Any carbon with a double bond, two hydrogens or two identical ring paths is out immediately.

Count the chain then the ring**
On the left, $CH(CH_2CH_2CH_3)(COOEt)(NH-)$ has four different groups so that is 1. Next, $CH(CH_3)(NH-)(CO-)$ has four different groups so that is 2. In the bicyclic octahydroindole part, the carbon bearing $-COOH$, the bridgehead $CH$ joined to $N$, and the other bridgehead $CH$ where the five and six membered rings join are each joined to four different groups. That adds 3 more, giving $2 + 3 = 5$ in total.

hints: Think about how a drug works in the body, receptors and enzymes are chiral protein structures so only one mirror image usually fits perfectly.
Think about what it takes in the factory to make only one mirror image instead of a 50:50 racemic mixture, separation, yield and special catalysts.
walkthrough:
Why shape matters in the body**
Enzymes and receptors are made from chiral amino acids, so their active sites are three dimensional chiral pockets. Think of a right hand fitting a right handed glove. Usually only one optical isomer of perindopril fits and binds effectively, the other may be inactive or even cause unwanted side effects.

Link single isomer to benefit**
If you supply only the active mirror image, every molecule can do its job. That means higher potency, you can give a smaller dose, and you avoid side effects that the wrong isomer might cause. This is the classic thalidomide lesson applied positively.

Link single isomer to cost**
Making one mirror image only is hard. Normal laboratory synthesis makes a racemic 50:50 mixture. To get a pure isomer you must either do a difficult separation or use a special chiral catalyst or enzyme, which cuts the yield of useful product in half and greatly increases cost and time.

Final answer: benefit: only the active stereoisomer is present so greater biological activity per gram, smaller dose needed and fewer side effects from the inactive / harmful isomer.
disadvantage: expensive and difficult to separate a single optical isomer from a racemic mixture, lower yield of useful product, may need expensive chiral catalyst or enzyme.

hints: Scan Fig. 6.1 from left to right for $C=O$ groups, decide in each case whether the $C=O$ carbon is joined to $-OR$, $-OH$ or $-N$.
Do not forget the nitrogen groups that contain no $C=O$, check the $N-H$ in the middle of the chain and the $N$ at the ring junction.
walkthrough:
Sort the three carbonyls**
There are three $C=O$ groups. On the far left, $CH_3CH_2O-C=O$ is $C$ joined to $O$-alkyl, that is an ester. On the far right, $HO-C=O$ is $C$ joined to $OH$, that is a carboxylic acid. In the middle right, $CH-C=O-N(ring)$ is $C$ joined to $N$, that is an amide, here a tertiary amide because the $N$ has no $H$.

Spot the amine**
In the middle of the chain, $-CH-NH-CH-$ has nitrogen joined only to carbon and hydrogen with no $C=O$, that is a secondary amine. So together you have four types: carboxylic acid, ester, amide and amine.
Final answer: carboxylic acid ($-COOH$), ester ($-COOR$), amide ($-CON<$) and (secondary) amine ($-NH-$).

hints: Mark the two bonds that water can split, the ester $COOEt$ on the left and the amide $CON$ linking the middle chain to the bicyclic ring.

Recall the products of complete acid hydrolysis, ester plus water gives carboxylic acid plus alcohol, amide plus water gives carboxylic acid plus amine (shown as neutral amine and acid for organic products).
Keep the central $-NH-$ untouched, it is an amine not an amide or ester, so the left and middle carbons stay joined together as one diacid fragment.
walkthrough:
Find what hydrolyses and what survives**
Put a circle around $CH_3CH_2O-CO-$ on the left, that is the ester link. Put a second circle around $-CO-N(ring)$ in the middle right, that is the amide link. The $-CH-NH-CH-$ in the centre is a simple amine link, it does not hydrolyse, so those two $CH$ carbons will remain connected.

Split the ester to ethanol plus acid**
Ester plus water gives acid plus alcohol: $$CH_3CH_2O-CO-R + H_2O \rightarrow R-COOH + CH_3CH_2OH$$ So the left end $EtOOC-CH(Pr)-$ becomes $HOOC-CH(Pr)-$ and you release $CH_3CH_2OH$. That is one of the three products counted.

Split the amide to acid plus amine**
Amide plus water gives acid plus amine: $$R-CO-N(ring) + H_2O \rightarrow R-COOH + HN(ring)$$ So the middle $-CH(CH_3)-CO-$ becomes $-CH(CH_3)-COOH$. Because the central $NH$ is untouched, the whole left plus middle piece becomes a single molecule: $$HOOC-CH(CH_2CH_2CH_3)-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH$$ This is essentially two linked amino acid residues.

Identify the released ring fragment**
The nitrogen side of the amide is the fused 5 and 6 membered ring system. After cleavage it becomes a secondary amine $>NH$ with its $-COOH$ group still attached at the adjacent carbon. That is octahydroindole-2-carboxylic acid, the third carbon skeleton product. Together with ethanol you have the three required organic products.

Final answer: Product 1: $HOOC-CH(CH_2CH_2CH_3)-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH$
Product 2: octahydroindole-2-carboxylic acid, the bicyclic secondary amine bearing $-COOH$ at C-2, with $NH$ at the ring junction.
Product 3: $CH_3CH_2OH$ ethanol.
